name: Amitriptyline + Chlordiazepoxide (Limbitrol)
summary: A fixed-dose combination of a tricyclic antidepressant and a benzodiazepine for moderate to severe depression with significant anxiety, with important risks of suicidality, dependence, and additive CNS and respiratory depression.
description: Limbitrol combines amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant that blocks the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, with chlordiazepoxide, a benzodiazepine that enhances GABAergic neurotransmission. It is indicated for moderate to severe depression associated with moderate to severe anxiety and is generally used short term. Because of suicidality warnings, dependence and withdrawal risks, and serious additive respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants, it is now used less often and frequently replaced by safer regimens.
patient_summary: Limbitrol is a combination medicine that treats both depression and anxiety. One part is an older antidepressant (amitriptyline), and the other part is a calming benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide). It can improve mood, worry, and tension, but it can also cause strong sleepiness, dizziness, dependence, and withdrawal if used for a long time or stopped suddenly. Taking it with opioids or alcohol can slow or stop breathing and can be life-threatening. It is not approved for children, and older adults have higher risks of confusion and falls. It should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time and only stopped with a doctor’s guidance.

primary_indications: Moderate to severe depression associated with moderate to severe anxiety
off_label_uses: Short-term symptomatic relief of anxiety and insomnia in patients with comorbid depressive disorders

linked_conditions.context: Treatment of moderate to severe major depressive episodes with prominent anxiety or agitation.
Short-term treatment of anxiety symptoms when comorbid with depressive illness.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amitriptyline, chlordiazepoxide, benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, or any component of the formulation
Coadministration with or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or MAO-B inhibitors at antidepressant doses
Acute recovery phase following myocardial infarction
Serious respiratory compromise (for example severe COPD, sleep apnea) unless benefits clearly outweigh risks
History of benzodiazepine or other substance use disorder, unless benefits clearly outweigh risks
monitoring_required: Mental status, depression severity, and suicidal ideation, especially at initiation and with dose changes
Emergence or worsening of anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, irritability, hostility, hypomania, mania, or other behavior changes
Sedation, psychomotor impairment, and fall risk, especially in older or debilitated patients
Respiratory status when combined with opioids, alcohol, or other CNS depressants, or in patients with respiratory disease
Heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG in older adults or patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease
Weight and BMI, and blood glucose in patients with diabetes or at metabolic risk
Liver and renal function tests and complete blood count with prolonged therapy
Serum sodium in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretic use, low body weight, volume depletion)
Signs and symptoms of benzodiazepine misuse, abuse, dependence, and withdrawal

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Significant vs placebo at week 1; ≥ amitriptyline alone; > chlordiazepoxide alone at weeks 2–4
efficacy_response.patient_text: In a 4-week study of adults with depression, Limbitrol worked better than placebo, and overall it worked at least as well as amitriptyline alone. It was clearly better than the tranquilizer part alone, especially later in treatment.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Amitriptyline is extensively metabolized hepatically (primarily via CYP2D6 and other CYP isoenzymes) to active metabolites; chlordiazepoxide is hepatically metabolized to long-acting active metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily renal elimination of metabolites; minor fecal excretion.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Component-dependent; amitriptyline and its metabolites have long and variable half-lives, and chlordiazepoxide and its metabolites have prolonged half-lives, increasing accumulation risk in older adults and hepatic impairment.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: High plasma protein binding for amitriptyline; moderate binding for chlordiazepoxide.

sections.heading: Primary Uses
sections.text: Limbitrol is indicated for moderate to severe depression when significant anxiety or nervous tension is also present. Because of safety concerns (suicidality, anticholinergic burden, benzodiazepine dependence, respiratory depression with other sedatives), it is generally reserved for selected cases and used for limited durations.
items: Treatment of moderate to severe {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder} associated with moderate to severe anxiety.
Depression with prominent agitation, tension, or nervousness when a combination of a tricyclic antidepressant and a benzodiazepine is judged appropriate.
off_label: Short-term management of anxiety and insomnia in patients with depressive disorders when other options are not suitable.
sections.patient_text: Limbitrol is mainly used when someone has both depression and significant anxiety or nervous tension. It is usually used for a limited time while other long-term treatments, such as a different antidepressant and therapy, are put in place.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but common themes from patients taking Limbitrol for depression with anxiety include:

quotes: The anxiety eased within the first few days, but I also felt very sleepy.
My nerves felt quieter, but I wanted to nap more than usual.
It helped me get through the evenings when my anxiety and low mood were worst.
items.note: The benzodiazepine component often produces noticeable calming and drowsiness early in treatment.

quotes: The constant heaviness started to lift after a couple of weeks.
I still had bad days, but the lows weren’t as deep or as long.
The combination seemed to help both my worry and my mood together.
items.note: Antidepressant effects from the tricyclic component typically emerge over 2–4 weeks.

quotes: I felt a bit foggy and unsteady, especially when I stood up quickly.
My mouth was dry all the time and I was a little constipated.
I noticed more trouble with memory and focus if I took higher doses.
When we tried to stop it too quickly, my anxiety bounced back hard.
Missing doses made me feel jittery and on edge.
My doctor warned me we’d have to taper slowly because of the tranquilizer part.
items.note: Because of the benzodiazepine component, dependence and withdrawal are real risks with longer-term or higher-dose use.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Limbitrol combines a fast-acting benzodiazepine component with a slower-onset tricyclic antidepressant component.
key_points: Hours to days: Anxiolytic and sedative effects from the chlordiazepoxide component may be noticed within the first few doses.
1–2 weeks: Early improvement in sleep, tension, and overall anxiety is common.
2–4 weeks: Antidepressant effects from the amitriptyline component typically emerge.
Long half-lives: Both components and their metabolites can accumulate, especially in older adults and those with liver impairment, increasing sedation and side-effect risk.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: In a trial of 279 adults with depression, Limbitrol was at least as effective as amitriptyline alone and clearly superior to chlordiazepoxide alone. In patients with both severe depression and anxiety, Limbitrol outperformed amitriptyline monotherapy.
sections.clinical_details: Feighner et al. (1979) conducted a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 279 adults with primary depressive illness, comparing Limbitrol (amitriptyline/chlordiazepoxide) with amitriptyline alone, chlordiazepoxide alone, and placebo over 4 weeks. The study used multiple rating scales including the Hamilton Depression Scale, Beck Depression Inventory, and physician and patient global assessments. Results showed statistically significant antidepressant benefit for Limbitrol versus placebo from week 1 onward (p<0.05), with efficacy that was at least comparable to amitriptyline monotherapy and superior to chlordiazepoxide monotherapy at later time points.

citation.authors: Feighner JP, Gardner EA, Johnston JA, et al.
citation.title: A placebo-controlled multicenter trial of Limbitrol versus its components in depressive illness

sections.heading: Warnings & Precautions ⚠️
sections.highlight: Carries both antidepressant suicidality risk and benzodiazepine-related risks of dependence, misuse, and life-threatening respiratory depression with opioids or alcohol.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. The risk may be higher in people who have had suicidal thoughts or actions before. All patients starting antidepressants should be closely watched for clinical worsening and suicidality, particularly during the first few months of therapy or at times of dose changes. Limbitrol is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Concomitant use with opioids: Combined use of benzodiazepines and opioids can result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve co-prescribing for patients in whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Use the lowest effective doses and shortest possible duration, and monitor patients for respiratory depression and excessive sedation.

Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Benzodiazepines, including chlordiazepoxide, expose users to risks of abuse, misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death. These risks are higher when combined with alcohol, other CNS depressants, or illicit substances. Assess each patient’s risk before starting therapy and monitor regularly.

Dependence and withdrawal: Continued benzodiazepine use may cause clinically significant physical dependence. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction after prolonged use can cause acute withdrawal reactions, including seizures, severe anxiety, agitation, and other serious symptoms. Taper gradually under medical supervision.

Anticholinergic burden: Amitriptyline has potent anticholinergic properties, increasing the risk of constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth, confusion, and heat intolerance. Use caution in patients with glaucoma, urinary retention, decreased GI motility, BPH, or cognitive impairment.
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Limbitrol can cause orthostatic hypotension and marked sedation, leading to falls and fractures, especially in older adults and frail patients.

CNS depression: May impair mental and physical abilities required for tasks such as driving or operating machinery. Effects are stronger with alcohol, cannabis, opioids, other sedative-hypnotics, or antihistamines.
Serotonin syndrome: Use with other serotonergic agents or MAOIs increases the risk of potentially life-threatening serotonin syndrome. Avoid contraindicated combinations and monitor for symptoms.
Hyponatremia and SIADH: Antidepressants, including TCAs, have been associated with hyponatremia, particularly in older adults or patients taking diuretics or who are volume depleted.

Cardiovascular risk: Amitriptyline may precipitate conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias, especially in patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease or those taking other QT-prolonging or pro-arrhythmic drugs.

Mania or hypomania: Antidepressants can precipitate a switch to mania or hypomania in patients with bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar disorder before starting therapy and monitor for mood switching.

Perioperative considerations: Stopping high-dose or long-term therapy abruptly before surgery may cause withdrawal; continuation may increase arrhythmia and drug interaction risk. Individualize per patient.

Older adults: Amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide are Beers Criteria high-risk medications; avoid when possible in adults 65 years and older because of strong anticholinergic effects, sedation, fall risk, and risk of dependence.
patient_counseling: Tell your doctor right away about new or worse depression, anxiety, panic attacks, irritability, or any thoughts of self-harm.
Do not drink alcohol or use street drugs while taking this medicine.
Do not take more than prescribed, and do not share this medicine with anyone.
Do not stop this medicine suddenly; your doctor will help you slowly lower the dose.
Call emergency services right away if you or someone caring for you notices slow or difficult breathing, extreme sleepiness, or trouble waking you up, especially if you also take opioids.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common side effects reflect both tricyclic antidepressant anticholinergic effects and benzodiazepine-related sedation and cognitive slowing. Serious risks include suicidality, arrhythmias, serotonin syndrome, severe skin reactions, and life-threatening respiratory depression with other sedatives.
plain_language_list: Drowsiness, sleepiness, or feeling weak or tired
Dizziness or feeling lightheaded (especially when standing up)
Stomach upset, nausea, or decreased appetite
Strange or vivid dreams, restlessness or agitation

common.patient_note: Very common, especially when starting treatment or after dose increases.
Can increase the risk of falls, particularly in older adults.
May be managed with sugar-free gum or sips of water; report if severe.

common.symptom: Constipation, stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, or decreased appetite
Restlessness or strange or vivid dreams

less_common: Orthostatic hypotension and fainting, especially in older adults
Confusion, memory problems, or difficulty concentrating
Trouble passing urine or urinary retention
Sexual dysfunction or change in sex interest
serious: Suicidal thoughts or actions, especially in children, adolescents, and young adults
Severe allergic reactions (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing)
Severe blood pressure changes, stroke-like symptoms, chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeat
Very low sodium levels (confusion, seizures, change in balance)
Severe constipation or abdominal pain suggesting a serious bowel problem
Severe liver problems (yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe fatigue, abdominal pain)
Serotonin syndrome when used with other serotonergic drugs (agitation, fever, tremor, sweating, diarrhea)
Severe skin reactions with fever or blistering (Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS)
Severe respiratory depression or coma, especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives
sections.patient_text: Many people have some sleepiness, dizziness, dry mouth, or stomach upset when starting Limbitrol. Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, severe rash, thoughts of self-harm, or sudden behavior or mood changes.

sections.heading: Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Limbitrol has important interaction risks from both its tricyclic and benzodiazepine components, including life-threatening respiratory depression with opioids and serious serotonin or cardiovascular effects with other psychotropics.

items.with: Opioid agonists (for example codeine, oxycodone, morphine, methadone, hydrocodone, fentanyl)
items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
items.action: Avoid combination when possible. If necessary, use lowest effective doses and shortest duration; monitor closely and consider prescribing an opioid overdose reversal agent.

items.with: Alcohol and other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, barbiturates, gabapentinoids, many antihistamines)
items.risk: Additive CNS and respiratory depression and impaired coordination.
items.action: Avoid or minimize use; counsel patients to avoid alcohol and sedating over-the-counter products.

items.with: MAOIs (isocarboxazid, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, rasagiline) and linezolid or IV methylene blue
items.risk: Hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome, severe CNS toxicity.
items.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between discontinuing an MAOI and starting Limbitrol, and 14 days between stopping Limbitrol and starting an MAOI.

items.with: Serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, other TCAs, triptans, buspirone, fentanyl, tramadol, St John’s wort, dextromethorphan, certain migraine or pain medications)
items.action: Use with caution; avoid high-risk combinations; monitor for serotonin syndrome symptoms.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors (for example fluoxetine, paroxetine, duloxetine, bupropion, quinidine)
items.action: Consider lower amitriptyline dose and monitor for anticholinergic and cardiac side effects.

items.with: CYP3A4 inhibitors (for example cimetidine, certain azole antifungals, some macrolide antibiotics)
items.risk: Increased chlordiazepoxide concentrations and prolonged sedation.
items.action: Monitor closely and consider dose reduction.

items.with: Other QT-prolonging or arrhythmogenic drugs (for example certain antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones)
items.risk: Additive risk of QT prolongation and serious ventricular arrhythmias.
items.action: Avoid when possible; if combination is necessary, monitor ECG and electrolytes.

items.with: Anticholinergic agents (for example many antipsychotics, antiparkinsonian agents, some antihistamines, bladder antimuscarinics)
items.risk: Additive anticholinergic toxicity (constipation, urinary retention, confusion, blurred vision).
items.action: Use with caution; monitor for severe anticholinergic effects.

items.risk: Altered blood pressure control, enhanced hypotension, or loss of antihypertensive effect.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure and adjust doses as necessary.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Both the benzodiazepine and tricyclic components should be tapered gradually after prolonged use. Tapering schedules should be individualized based on duration of use, dose, comorbidities, and prior history of withdrawal. Rapid dose reductions or abrupt discontinuation may precipitate withdrawal symptoms, which can be severe or life-threatening.
key_points: Benzodiazepine withdrawal: Abrupt chlordiazepoxide discontinuation after prolonged use can cause severe anxiety, insomnia, tremor, agitation, and seizures.
TCA discontinuation: Sudden amitriptyline withdrawal can cause flu-like symptoms, insomnia, irritability, and cholinergic rebound.
Taper plan: Gradual dose reduction over weeks to months, with smaller decrements as lower doses are reached.
High-risk groups: Long-term users, high doses, older adults, and those with seizure history or substance use disorders require slower tapers and closer monitoring.
sections.patient_text: Do not stop Limbitrol suddenly. Your doctor will help you slowly reduce the dose to lower the risk of withdrawal symptoms like anxiety, trouble sleeping, shaking, or seizures, and to reduce the chance that your depression or anxiety will suddenly return.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Limbitrol dosing is based on symptom severity, tolerability, and clinical judgment. The goal is to use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration, especially in older adults and those at higher risk for adverse effects or dependence.

adult.start: 3 or 4 tablets daily in one or more divided doses (each tablet containing amitriptyline 12.5 mg with chlordiazepoxide 5 mg, or amitriptyline 25 mg with chlordiazepoxide 10 mg).
adult.titrate: Increase or decrease based on clinical response and tolerability; typically used short term (for example 4 to 6 weeks) while transitioning to or optimizing a longer-term antidepressant regimen.
adult.usual_range: 2 to 6 tablets daily in one or more divided doses.
adult.max: Maximum daily dose approximately amitriptyline 150 mg and chlordiazepoxide 60 mg.
adult.notes: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, especially in older adults and in patients at risk for respiratory depression, falls, substance use disorder, or severe adverse effects.

sections.patient_text: Your dose depends on how severe your symptoms are. The total amount is usually split into doses during the day, with a larger part often taken at bedtime to help limit daytime sleepiness. Doctors aim for the smallest dose that works and try to avoid long-term use.

renal_adjustments.dose: No specific dosage adjustment is provided in labeling; use with caution, especially in moderate to severe impairment.
renal_adjustments.patient_note: Kidney problems usually do not require a strict dose change, but your doctor may still start low and monitor you closely.

hepatic_adjustments.dose: Use with caution. Lower initial and maintenance doses are often recommended for tricyclic antidepressants because clearance is reduced and the therapeutic index is narrow.
hepatic_adjustments.patient_note: If you have liver problems, your dose may need to be lower and increased very slowly.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Limbitrol combines a tricyclic antidepressant with a benzodiazepine, both of which have important considerations in pregnancy, breastfeeding, pediatrics, and older adults.
sections.pregnancy: Use during pregnancy only if potential benefits justify potential fetal risks. Late pregnancy exposure to benzodiazepines and tricyclic antidepressants may increase the risk of neonatal respiratory depression, feeding difficulties, low body temperature, and withdrawal symptoms.
sections.lactation: Both amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide are excreted in breast milk. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended while taking this combination. A decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother.
sections.pediatrics: Limbitrol is not approved for use in pediatric patients. Antidepressants carry an increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children and adolescents.
sections.geriatrics: Amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide are Beers Criteria high-risk medications. Older adults have increased sensitivity to anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, cognitive impairment, sedation, falls, fractures, and benzodiazepine dependence. Avoid when possible; if used, employ very low doses, slow titration, and close monitoring.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood, anxiety symptoms, and suicidal ideation, particularly during initiation and dose changes.
Level of sedation, psychomotor impairment, and fall risk, especially in older adults.
Respiratory rate and depth when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants.
Heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG in patients with cardiac risk factors or on other QT-prolonging drugs.
Weight, BMI, and blood glucose as clinically indicated.
Liver and renal function tests and complete blood count with prolonged therapy.
Serum sodium in at-risk patients for hyponatremia.
Signs of serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs.
Evidence of misuse, abuse, or development of benzodiazepine use disorder.
Symptoms of withdrawal during tapering or after dose reductions.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Limbitrol is supplied as fixed-dose oral tablets containing both amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide.
items: Tablets, oral: Amitriptyline HCl 12.5 mg and chlordiazepoxide 5 mg.
Tablets, oral: Amitriptyline HCl 25 mg and chlordiazepoxide 10 mg.
Generic equivalents available in similar strengths.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant that inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, increasing synaptic monoamine levels and improving mood and certain anxiety symptoms. Chlordiazepoxide is a benzodiazepine that binds to benzodiazepine sites on the GABA-A receptor complex, enhancing GABA’s inhibitory effects and producing anxiolytic, sedative, and muscle-relaxant actions. Together, these mechanisms target both depressive and anxiety symptoms but also increase the risk of sedation, cognitive impairment, dependence, and withdrawal.
sections.patient_text: One part of this medicine boosts brain chemicals that affect mood, and the other part calms the brain and body. This can help both depression and anxiety, but it also makes the medicine more sedating and more likely to cause dependence if used for a long time.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Limbitrol is best suited for short-term treatment of moderate to severe depression with significant anxiety while a safer long-term antidepressant regimen and non-pharmacologic therapy are established. Because of benzodiazepine-related risks (dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, falls) and the anticholinergic burden of amitriptyline, many clinicians prefer SSRIs or SNRIs plus non-benzodiazepine strategies. Reserve use for patients in whom alternative treatments are ineffective, poorly tolerated, or contraindicated, and reassess the need for ongoing benzodiazepine treatment frequently. Careful screening for bipolar disorder is essential before prescribing, and separating the antidepressant and benzodiazepine components (for example SSRI plus short-term benzodiazepine) may offer greater flexibility in dosing and tapering.

sections.heading: Availability and Regulatory Status
sections.text: Limbitrol is a branded fixed-dose combination of amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide, originally approved in the United States in the 1970s. Generic formulations containing the same strengths of amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide are available. Use has declined with the broader availability of SSRIs, SNRIs, and non-benzodiazepine regimens for depression and anxiety.

seo.title: Amitriptyline + Chlordiazepoxide (Limbitrol): Dosing, Opioid Risks, Dependence and Safety Guide
seo.description: Clinical guide to Limbitrol, a combination of amitriptyline and chlordiazepoxide for depression with anxiety. Covers study data, dosing ranges (2–6 tablets/day), benzodiazepine dependence and withdrawal, black box suicidality warning, and serious risks with opioids and other sedatives.

editorial.reviewStatement: This content has been medically reviewed by board-certified psychiatrists and cross-checked against FDA labeling and key clinical trial data.

faqs.a: Limbitrol is a combination of amitriptyline (a tricyclic antidepressant) and chlordiazepoxide (a benzodiazepine). It is used to treat moderate to severe depression that occurs with significant anxiety or nervous tension. It is usually used short term while longer-term treatments such as other antidepressants and therapy are put into place.

faqs.q: Is Limbitrol safe to take with opioids or alcohol?
faqs.a: Limbitrol should not be taken with alcohol or misused with opioids. The benzodiazepine component can interact with opioids and alcohol to cause extreme sleepiness, slow or shallow breathing, coma, or even death. If Limbitrol must be used with an opioid, it should be at the lowest effective doses and for the shortest possible time under close medical supervision.

faqs.q: Can Limbitrol cause dependence or withdrawal?
faqs.a: Yes. The benzodiazepine component (chlordiazepoxide) can cause physical dependence, especially with higher doses or longer-term use. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, tremor, and in severe cases seizures or severe behavior changes. The amitriptyline component can also cause a discontinuation syndrome if stopped abruptly. Limbitrol should always be tapered slowly under a doctor’s guidance.

faqs.q: How long can I stay on Limbitrol?
faqs.a: Limbitrol is generally intended for short-term use. Many patients take it for several weeks while a longer-term antidepressant regimen is started or adjusted. Ongoing use should be regularly reviewed with your doctor. If you have been taking it for a long time, the dose should be tapered slowly to avoid withdrawal and rebound symptoms.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose of Limbitrol?
faqs.a: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once or extra doses to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure, contact your doctor or pharmacist for advice.
